summary: Wattenberger opens with a historical analogy: early-1900s accounting was tedious manual work, but the 1979 spreadsheet transformed the field not by automating calculations—calculators already did that—but by providing a structured interface that stacked calculations into live-updating formulas, freeing accountants to focus on the numbers. She reframes the automation-versus-augmentation dichotomy, arguing they are deeply related: augmentation is composed of smaller automations. Automating sub-tasks like data aggregation or visualization serves a greater augmentative goal such as analysis. She contends that chatbots alone are not the future; embedding AI into structured interfaces where users still drive is more powerful. She then introduces the ladder of abstraction, illustrated through Google Maps, where the same area appears differently at each zoom level with detail selectively hidden to match the task. She demonstrates a prototype on Peter Pan: an LLM summarizes paragraphs to single sentences, groups of paragraphs, and entire chapters, enabling a writer to adjust pacing or plot at a high level before zooming back to raw text, also referencing Kurt Vonnegut's graphical story arcs. Combining augmentation-as-stacked-automations with abstraction-level traversal, she describes Adept.ai's mission to train AI to use software like humans. She presents a multi-level hypothetical Airbnb interface: individual listing views side by side, a table view for 50 listings with decision factors laid out, and a scatter plot where listings appear as circles colored by Wi-Fi reviews, positioned by price (left to right) and proximity to the hotel (bottom). Crucially, users can act from any level—booking from the table view, or circling listings on the scatter plot to message hosts about early check-in. She credits Bret Victor's talk 'Up and Down the Ladder of Abstraction,' clarifying her argument is not that higher levels are better but that AI can generate different levels, glue them together, and make it easy to move between them. She closes with three takeaways: augmenting tasks look like automating smaller tedious parts (spreadsheets didn't replace accountants); we think about information at different abstraction levels and AI can generate and act on those levels; and this is the thinking at Adept.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Accounting and the Spreadsheet Revolution
sections.summary: Wattenberger uses early-1900s accounting as a frustration baseline, then introduces VisiCalc (1979) and Lotus 1-2-3 as transformative not because they automated calculations but because their structured interface stacked calculations into live-updating formulas, freeing accountants to focus on the numbers.

sections.title: Reframing Automation vs. Augmentation
sections.summary: She challenges the automation-versus-augmentation dichotomy, arguing augmentation is composed of smaller automations. Automating tedious sub-tasks serves augmentative goals. She contends chatbots alone are not the future; embedding AI into structured interfaces where users still drive is more powerful.

sections.title: The Ladder of Abstraction
sections.summary: Wattenberger introduces the ladder of abstraction via Google Maps: the same area is represented at different detail levels, with information selectively hidden to suit navigation, restaurant-finding, or long-range travel. She asks whether AI can bring these principles to other interfaces.

sections.title: Zooming Out on Books and Story Arcs
sections.summary: She demos a Peter Pan prototype where an LLM summarizes paragraphs, groups of paragraphs, and chapters at successive zoom levels, enabling pacing and plot editing at a high level. She also references Kurt Vonnegut's graphical story arcs as another high-level text representation.

sections.title: Combining Concepts: Adept and the Airbnb Demo
sections.summary: Combining augmentation-as-stacked-automations with abstraction-level traversal, Wattenberger describes Adept.ai's mission to train AI to use software like humans. She presents a hypothetical Airbnb interface that extracts user-specific criteria (walking distance, transit, Wi-Fi reviews, key photos) while preserving the ability to book or message directly from the elevated view.

sections.title: Scaling the Airbnb Demo Across Abstraction Levels
sections.summary: Wattenberger extends the Airbnb demo across multiple zoom levels: side-by-side individual listing views for comparison, a table view of 50 listings with decision factors for quick eyeballing, and a scatter plot where listings are circles colored by Wi-Fi reviews, positioned by price and proximity to the hotel. She emphasizes that users can act from any level—booking from the table or batch-messaging hosts from the scatter plot about early check-in. She notes we currently manually abstract this information in our heads, which costs mental energy. She credits Bret Victor's 'Up and Down the Ladder of Abstraction,' clarifying her argument is not that higher levels are better but that AI can generate different levels, glue them together, and enable easy movement between them.

sections.title: Three Takeaways and Closing
sections.summary: Wattenberger closes with three takeaways: augmenting tasks will look like automating smaller tedious parts (no one sees spreadsheets as job-replacing); we think about information at different abstraction levels and should use AI to generate and act on those levels; and this is the thinking at Adept. She invites the audience to follow Adept's work.
